title: Which luxury watch fits your monthly budget?
lead: Thinking in monthly instalments instead of sticker prices changes which watches are actually within reach. A quick tour of what each budget unlocks.
body: Most people look at a luxury watch and see one number: the full price. But once financing at 0% enters the picture, the more useful question becomes what you are comfortable setting aside each month. Over 48 months, a CHF 3'000 watch costs about as much per month as a streaming bundle and a gym membership.

Under CHF 100 a month, Swiss houses like Alpina, Frederique Constant or Maurice Lacroix offer mechanical watches with real pedigree and classic proportions. Between CHF 100 and 200, the field opens up to Oris divers, Longines heritage pieces and entry references from Tudor — watches you can wear daily for decades.

From CHF 200 a month upwards you are in Omega, IWC, Panerai and Zenith territory: manufacture movements, recognisable designs and strong long-term desirability. The right choice is rarely the most expensive one — it is the one whose monthly cost you can forget about while enjoying the watch.

title: The Watch That Never Left Bond's Wrist
lead: From the Submariner of the novels to the titanium Seamaster of the latest films, 007's wrist tells its own story of watchmaking.
body: Ian Fleming wrote Bond as a Rolex man, and the early films kept it that way: a Submariner on a worn strap, a tool watch for a man with a dangerous job. The seventies flirted with digital Seikos, a period detail that dates those films as precisely as the cars.

Everything changed in 1995. From GoldenEye onwards, Bond has worn an Omega Seamaster — first the wave-dial 300M in blue, later Planet Ocean references, and most recently a titanium Seamaster 300M on a mesh bracelet, aged as if it had genuinely survived a naval career.

The logic is sound beyond marketing: a dive watch is legible, robust and unfussy — exactly the character. It is also a reminder that a great watch does not need to shout. It simply needs to be there, every scene, doing its job.

title: 5 Iconic Luxury Handbags Worth Knowing
lead: Icons are not declared, they are earned over decades. Five silhouettes that define what a luxury handbag can be.
body: The Chanel 2.55 practically invented the modern luxury bag: quilted leather, a chain strap that freed the hands, and a lock with its own mythology. Nearly seventy years on, it remains the reference point every flap bag is measured against.

Hermès contributes two icons. The Kelly, angular and formal, became famous on the arm of a princess; the Birkin, softer and roomier, turned scarcity itself into a design feature. Both are hand-built by a single artisan and hold value like few objects in fashion.

The Louis Vuitton Speedy brought travel-trunk craft to daily life, and the Lady Dior — architectural, cannage-quilted — proved a bag could be both jewellery and armour. Different houses, one lesson: an icon solves a real need with a shape you can recognise across a street.

title: Bringing Luxury Handbags Within Reach
lead: The same idea that works for watches — pay the fair price, spread over time — applied to the world's most coveted bags.
body: A great handbag shares a quality with a great watch: it outlives trends. Chanel flaps, Hermès leathers and Dior classics are carried for decades and passed on, which is precisely what makes them candidates for considered financing rather than impulse purchases.

Our approach stays identical to watches: the price on the tag is the price you pay, split into monthly instalments at 0% interest, with every piece checked for authenticity and condition before it ships.

The selection focuses deliberately on maisons whose bags have proven themselves over decades rather than seasons — because an instalment plan only makes sense on something you will still love when the last payment clears.

title: Beneath the Surface, the world of diving watches
lead: Born as professional tools in the 1950s, dive watches became the most versatile design in watchmaking. Here is what actually makes one.
body: The modern dive watch appeared in the early 1950s, when recreational and military diving created a need for instruments that could survive depth and remain legible in darkness. The formula crystallised fast: a high-contrast dial, luminous markers, and a bezel that rotates in one direction only — so a knock can only shorten a dive, never dangerously extend it.

Water-resistance figures deserve translation. 30 metres means rain; 100 metres means swimming; a truly dive-ready watch starts at 200 or 300 metres, built with screwed crowns and casebacks. Standards formalise the details, but the visible cues — bezel, lume, robust case — are what define the genre.

The irony of the dive watch is that its natural habitat became the office. Legibility, toughness and a design language everyone understands make it the one watch that works with a wetsuit and a suit alike — which is why nearly every serious collection starts with one.

title: LVMH Watch Week 2026
lead: January's first fixture keeps growing in relevance. What the group's houses signalled this year about where watchmaking is heading.
body: January belongs to LVMH Watch Week, the event where TAG Heuer, Hublot, Zenith and Bulgari open the year's conversation before the industry converges on Geneva in spring. Its role has changed over the editions: less a preview, more a statement of intent.

The direction across the houses is consistent — cases getting slightly smaller and thinner, colour used with intent rather than decoration, and in-house calibres appearing at prices where supplied movements were once the rule.

For buyers, weeks like this matter for a practical reason: they move the reference market. When a line is refreshed, the outgoing generation often becomes the smart purchase — same design language, proven reliability, better price.

title: NEW : TAG Heuer Connected Calibre E5
lead: The Connected line keeps arguing that a smartwatch can be built like a luxury watch. The Calibre E5 is its strongest case yet.
body: TAG Heuer's Connected series has always taken a contrarian position: build the smartwatch with the same materials, finishing and design language as a mechanical chronograph, and let the electronics be the part that changes.

The Calibre E5 generation continues that logic — sapphire glass, steel or titanium cases and interchangeable straps around an upgraded display and improved battery life, with sport tracking tuned for golf, running and daily fitness built in.

It will not replace a mechanical watch for collectors, and it does not try to. It is aimed at the wrist that spends the week between meetings and workouts — and wants one watch that looks right in both.

title: The art of complications
lead: In watchmaking, a complication is anything a watch does beyond telling the time. A guided tour from the date window to the minute repeater.
body: The word sounds like a problem, but in horology a complication is a promise: any function beyond hours, minutes and seconds. The humble date window is one. So is the chronograph you start at the airport gate, and the GMT hand that keeps home time while you travel.

Higher up the ladder live the poetic complications. The moonphase tracks the lunar cycle across a tiny painted sky; the perpetual calendar knows the length of every month, leap years included, and will not need correcting until 2100.

At the summit sit the tourbillon, invented to average out gravity's effect on precision, and the minute repeater, which chimes the time on demand. Their practical value today is almost nil — and that is the point. Complications are watchmaking arguing that difficulty, mastered, is beautiful.

title: The LOEV Story: Swiss Timeless Design Meets Purpose
lead: A young Swiss jewellery house built around a simple idea: engagement pieces with timeless design and transparent pricing.
body: LOEV approaches fine jewellery the way good watch design approaches a dial: remove everything that does not serve the piece. Its solitaires and pavé rings favour clean settings and classic proportions over seasonal flourish.
The house positions itself around transparency — in materials, in sourcing and in price — a stance that resonates with a generation that researches a ring the way it researches a watch movement.
It is a fitting presence in a catalogue built on lasting value: pieces designed to be worn for a lifetime, financed at the pace of a monthly instalment.

title: Watches and Wonders 2025: When Colour Redefines Time
lead: Geneva's great fair confirmed it: colour is no longer a novelty act. It has become a serious design language.
body: For decades the safe luxury dial came in three flavours: black, white, silver. Watches and Wonders 2025 made official what the market had been whispering — green, salmon, ice blue and deep burgundy have moved from limited-edition bait to core collection colours.

Colour changes how a watch is bought. A black dial is chosen with the head; a salmon dial is chosen with the gut. The houses know it, and the best of this year's releases used colour with restraint — one saturated dial against steel, not a costume.
For anyone building a collection, the advice writes itself: let the first watch be versatile, and let the second one be the colour you could not stop thinking about on the train home.
